1:
The date is fixed by everyone and agreed by none in detail. Gill reckons the tenth year from Jeconiah’s captivity, in the reign of Zedekiah, and names the month Tebet, answering to part of December and part of January; he also lists the variants, the Septuagint giving the twelfth year and the first day of the month, the Arabic version the twelfth month, the Vulgate Latin the eleventh day. Wesley says only that the year is of Jeconiah’s captivity. Ellicott dates it by the siege instead of the reign: a year and two days after the investment of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, about six months before the city fell and seven before it was destroyed. That places it, he argues, after the siege had been temporarily raised by the approach of the Egyptians under Pharaoh-Hophra and after Jeremiah had prophesied the failure of that attempt, probably just as news of the relief reached the exiles and gave them fresh hope.

Why the oracle stands where it does is answered the same way by Gill and Henry. Gill says the prophecy was delivered before the one concerning Tyre though placed after it, because fulfilled after it, Nebuchadnezzar being given Egypt as a reward for taking Tyre. Henry says the same and draws a moral from the moment: this first word against Egypt came just when the king of Egypt was coming to relieve Jerusalem, and did not answer the expectations the Jews had of him. It is good, Henry says, to foresee the failing of all our creature-confidences at the very time when we are most tempted to depend upon them, that we may cease from man. He notices a second difference of arrangement. The prophecy against Tyre began with the people and proceeded to the prince; this one begins with the prince, because it began to be accomplished in the insurrections of the people against the prince not long after.

Keil and Delitzsch stand back from the oracle to the shape of the whole. The announcement of judgment upon Egypt is proclaimed in seven words of God, the first five threats and the last two lamentations over the destruction of Pharaoh and of his imperial power. The first threatens Pharaoh and his people and land in grand and general traits; the second predicts specially the conquest and plundering of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar; the rest depict the day of judgment upon Egypt and its allies, the annihilation of Pharaoh’s might, and a warning drawn from the glory and overthrow of Assyria. The prophecy takes so elaborate a form, they say, because the prophet regards Pharaoh and Egypt as the embodiment of a whole phase of the imperial power. Clarke outlines the same ground more plainly: these chapters foretell the conquest accomplished in the twenty-seventh year of Jehoiachin’s captivity and foretold by Jeremiah also.

On the king himself they converge. Gill notes that Pharaoh was a name common to all the kings of Egypt, that this one was Pharaohhophra, and that Herodotus calls him Apries; Clarke identifies him the same way from the prophecies of Jeremiah. Clarke states the charge: the prophecy opens by charging the king with the same extravagant pride and profanity laid to the prince of Tyre before, since he appears to have affected divine honours and boasted of his kingdom’s strength so far that, as an ancient historian tells us, he impiously declared God himself could not dispossess him. Hence the prophet addresses him under the image of one of the crocodiles inhabiting the river of whose riches he vaunted, and assures him that with as much ease as a fisherman drags a hooked fish God would drag him and his people away. Henry draws the same figure with the question under it: what is the king of Egypt, in God’s account, but a great dragon, venomous and mischievous, lying in the midst of his rivers to play there?
3:
The creature in the river is named by three of the four. Clarke says the word should be translated crocodile, since that is a real animal, numerous in the Nile, whereas the dragon is fabulous, the original signifying any large animal; the crocodile was the emblem of Egypt, and the rivers are the branches by which the Nile empties into the sea, termed by the ancients the seven mouths. Ellicott agrees that it unquestionably means crocodile, the characteristic animal of Egypt, in some parts hated and destroyed, in some worshipped as a deity, but everywhere feared as the most powerful and destructive creature of the country; Egypt, a creation of the Nile and wholly dependent on it, is personified by that animal basking on the sand-banks. Wesley keeps the older word, saying that this prophet, like Isaiah, compares the Egyptian king to that devouring dragon, lying not only at rest but waiting for prey.

Ellicott places the boast historically. The phrase his rivers suits the dynasty of Pharaoh-Hophra, whose capital was Sais in the midst of the Delta, and the claim that the river is his own is characteristic of the pride of Hophra, who according to Herodotus was accustomed to say that not even a god could dispossess him; the whole dynasty, beginning with Psammeticus, improved the river and encouraged foreign commerce, acquiring great wealth. Wesley reads the claim as a claim to everything, my river meaning my kingdom, power, riches and forces. Gill hears it answered where the inhabitants come to know the Lord, who could eject their king and deliver him to his enemy though he had said no God could.

The hooks and the fish are worked out differently. Gill takes the allusion to fishhooks, which stick in the jaws and draw the fish out, and reads them as powerful princes and armies that should be the ruin of Pharaoh, naming Amasis at the head of the Cyreneans and Greeks, and Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott finds a more particular allusion, to the ancient way of taking and destroying the crocodile, otherwise invulnerable to their arms; and since the crocodile represents the royal power, the fish are the people dependent on him, so that Pharaoh shall not fall alone but drag his people into a common ruin. Wesley says the same briefly, the fish being the people and their sticking their adherence to their king. Clarke turns the figure the other way: since most fish are troubled by an insect that buries its head in the flesh under the scales and sucks out the vital juices, he makes the fish the common people and their sticking the insurrection by which Amasis, one of the king’s own generals, dethroned Apries.

The wilderness is placed by two and described by the rest. Gill puts it in the deserts of Lybia and Cyrene, where Hophra fought Amasis and the Egyptian army perished, only the king escaping, as a crocodile lives on land as well as in water; Wesley names the deserts of Libya and Syene instead, and says the army was left unburied, a prey to wild beasts and birds. Clarke adds that the king, having fled to Upper Egypt, was afterwards taken prisoner and strangled. Ellicott treats the open fields as synonymous with the wilderness, Pharaoh and his people uprooted from their power and given over for a spoil. On the staff of reed Clarke calls Egypt an inefficient and faithless ally: the Israelites expected assistance when Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem, and the Egyptians made a feint to help and then retired; Ellicott recalls the older description of trust in a broken reed, says the reference is to no single fact so much as a continual, repeated result, and renders the difficult clause about the loins as meaning that they shake, the reed breaking under the man who leans on it and piercing his shoulder as he falls.
8:
Henry reads this as the plain statement of what the figure meant. The threatening is full and particular, and the sin bringing the ruin is pride: they said the river is mine and I have made it, therefore their land shall spue them out. God is against both king and people, against thee and against thy rivers, waters signifying people and multitudes. Multitudes will be cut off by the sword of civil war; the country will be depopulated, the land left uncultivated and the cities uninhabited. Their wealth was their pride, Henry says, and God will take it away; the land will be wastes of waste, as the margin reads it, desolate in the midst of countries that are so, and this the effect not so much of the wars they made as of the war the king of Babylon made upon them. The sin of pride, he concludes, is enough to ruin a whole nation. Gill names the same two grounds, the king’s pride in asserting the river to be his own and made by him for himself, and his perfidy to the house of Israel. Ellicott adds that the verse division is unfortunate, since the formula that they shall know that I am the Lord always closes a train of thought in this prophet; the new sentence begins with the reason for the judgment, which is pride.

The extent of the ruin turns on two place-names. Clarke reads the phrase as from Migdol to Syene, and describes Syene, now called Essuan, as the last city in Egypt towards Ethiopia, famous for a well into which the sun fell perpendicularly at midday. Ellicott argues the same: the word translated tower is a proper name, Migdol, a town near Suez, and Syene carries the affix denoting towards, so the rendering should be from Migdol to Syene, even unto the border of Ethiopia, which is to say the whole length of the land, Syene being the southern border town represented by the modern Assouan. Wesley reaches the same result without the philology, taking Syene for the boundary between Ethiopia and Egypt and the phrase for all Egypt.

The forty years are read three ways. Clarke makes them historical and exact: the country from Migdol was so completely ruined that it might well be called desert, and the desolation probably continued through the whole reign of Amasis, which was just forty years. Wesley counts them differently, from about the thirtieth year of Jeconiah’s captivity to the seventieth, which was the first of Cyrus. Ellicott denies that any such period can be found. The desolation predicted, taken in the literal sense of the words, has certainly never been fulfilled, and no definite forty years can be made out from history; the two difficulties go together, and the first is explained by the second. This prophet elsewhere represents the calamity of Judah in the historic terms of their former suffering in the wilderness, intending neither a specific time nor a precise repetition, and does the same here: the people pass into a condition like that of the Israelites in the wilderness, expressed in strong concrete terms whose literal fulfilment was neither intended nor expected. Gill limits the words more mildly: they must be understood not strictly but with some limitation, since it cannot be thought no single passenger was left, but rather that few inhabited it and scarce any came for traffic.

On the scattering they agree in kind. Ellicott reports that Megasthenes and Berosus state that Nebuchadnezzar sent great numbers captive to Babylon, while others took refuge in Ethiopia, Libya and neighbouring lands; the desolation foretold is of the same kind as that of other countries that fell under a conqueror, plundered and reduced to subjection. Henry likewise ends with the people dispersed and scattered among the nations, and Gill sets Egypt among the countries made desolate by the king of Babylon.
13:
The forty years are counted again, and the two who count them differ. Gill reckons from the devastation by Nebuchadnezzar to the taking of Babylon by Cyrus. Clarke reckons from the commencement of the war against Pharaoh-hophra to the third or fourth year of Cyrus, and adds the probable occasion of the return, that Cyrus gave the Egyptians whom Nebuchadnezzar had brought to Babylon permission to go home. Gill adds that what is done by men under divine providence is said to be done by the Lord, though by the means of Cyrus. Keil and Delitzsch tie the promise to the threat by the particle that opens it, which refers back to the time already indicated: for forty years Egypt shall be utterly laid waste, and after that period the Lord will gather the Egyptians from their dispersion and turn their captivity, which is to say put an end to their suffering.

Where they return is disputed. Clarke reports that Pathros is supposed to mean the Delta, the country between the branches of the Nile named from the Greek letter it resembles, but says it may mean the Pathrusim in Upper Egypt near the Thebaid, which he thinks most likely. Ellicott takes the second without hesitation: Pathros is Upper Egypt, the Thebaid, called in the next clause the land of their birth and held by ancient testimony and many moderns to be the original seat of Egyptian power; he allows that it may be put only as the part for the whole. Wesley agrees, calling it the southern part of Egypt, where stood the famous city Thebae known for its hundred gates, the ancient habitation of their fathers.

On the baseness of the restored kingdom all say the same thing and prove it differently. Wesley reads the word plainly as low, tributary and dependent, granting that in the times of the Ptolemeys Egypt was considerable, but even then it did not rule the nations about her. Gill says the same of the empires it belonged to, the Persian and then the Macedonian, under which it was kept down more than the rest lest it regain its former strength and glory; it grew more famous under some of the Ptolemies but never recovered its greatness. Ellicott states the principle: Egypt should be restored, but not to its power, and historically this has been eminently true, for it struggled a little while against its oppressors but its power was already broken, and since its conquest by Cambyses it has never been long independent. There are few stronger contrasts in any inhabited country, he says, than between the ancient glory and wealth of Egypt and its later insignificance. Clarke turns the claim into a list, tracing the tribute through the Babylonians under Amasis, the Persians, the Macedonians, the Romans, the Saracens, the Mameluke slaves, and finally Selim, who annexed Egypt to the Ottoman empire, of which Clarke says it still continues a province governed by a pacha and twenty-four beys advanced from servitude.

The last clause turns the judgment back on Israel, where Ellicott is fullest. The result for God’s people is that a standing temptation is removed: they had continually transgressed by looking to Egypt for aid, and that trust kept bringing their iniquity to remembrance, both by being against the express command of God and by involving treachery against the power they were subject to. Gill reaches the same end from the history: Egypt having been treacherous to them and then subdued by the Chaldeans, the Jews after their return put no more confidence in it, since it had become what the prophecy said it would be, weaker and more abject than the rest and despised by its neighbours. Wesley states it most sharply: the sinful reliance on the arm of flesh provoked God to call to mind their other iniquities, and the looking to Egypt was a forgetting of God.
17:
The date of this second oracle is remarked on by all, being so late. Clarke gives it as the twenty-seventh year of Jeconiah’s captivity, fifteen years after the taking of Jerusalem and sixteen after the earlier prophecy of this chapter, and says it is supposed to be the last the prophet wrote. Ellicott calls it the latest date among all his prophecies, the thirty-fifth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, uttered after the close of the siege of Tyre. Wesley says simply the year after the conquest of Tyre. Gill alone leaves the reckoning open, since Jarchi, Kimchi and Abendana take the year to be of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign rather than of the captivity, though he notes that Tyre was taken in the thirty-fifth year of that reign.

Henry and Ellicott explain why so late an oracle stands here. It comes in here, Henry says, for the explication of all that was said against Egypt, and being the last prophecy we have of this prophet it should have stood last in the book, but is laid here so that the prophecies against Egypt might come together; Ellicott adds that it is set here so that the mention of the agent of the conquest should follow immediately on the general prophecy of judgment.

The two also fill in the intervening years, and differ on whether they fit. Henry has Nebuchadnezzar spend two or three campaigns after the fall of Jerusalem on the Ammonites and Moabites, then thirteen years besieging Tyre, while the Egyptians warred with the Cyrenians and with one another and were much weakened; at the end of the siege the word comes, that the destruction foretold sixteen years before and only partly accomplished should now be finished. Ellicott works the same chronology harder and finds a gap. Since the siege lasted thirteen years it must have begun within three years of the fall of Jerusalem; but Josephus states that in his twenty-third year Nebuchadnezzar made a successful expedition northward, then subdued the Ammonites and Moabites, and then conquered Egypt. The two earlier campaigns are consistent with a siege still in progress, he says, but hardly the last, so a considerable interval must be supposed, of which Josephus takes no notice; the utterance most probably falls in the early part of the campaign against Egypt.

On the hard service Clarke is the most physical, with the soldiers continually on duty, their heads made bald by wearing helmets and their shoulders peeled by carrying baskets of earth to the fortifications and wood for towers; Wesley calls the thirteen years a great service to the justice of God, and says only the king’s immovable resolution kept a weary army to it. On the lost wages they part company. Clarke says the Tyrians, finding the city impossible to defend, put all their wealth aboard their vessels and escaped, so that Nebuchadnezzar lost the spoil of one of the richest cities in the world; Wesley allows that much wealth was carried away and much wasted during the siege, but has what was left preserved by articles of surrender. Ellicott meets the harder question the verse raises. It has been argued from the silence of history about the siege that Nebuchadnezzar never took the city at all; but all that is meant, he says, is that he obtained no considerable booty, the Tyrians having had warning and opportunity to convey their valuables by sea. Jerome asserts that they did so, and describes the capture as made by building a mole from the mainland to the island, the means Alexander used afterwards, which explains the bald heads and peeled shoulders. Berosus testifies that Nebuchadnezzar conquered all Syria; besides, it is inconceivable that a prophet who long survived the siege should have left this prophecy on record if the event had fallen out otherwise. Gill notes only that both spellings of the king’s name are used in Scripture.
19:
The wages are given, and the credit is divided. Gill opens with the ground of the grant, that the king of Babylon had been working for nothing and had spent much blood and treasure to little advantage; and he insists that the gift was not to Nebuchadnezzar merely but to his army also, who did the main of the labour and had the plunder for it, though the kingdom itself was annexed to their king’s monarchy. Clarke states it simply, that because he fulfilled the designs of God against Tyre, God rewards him with the spoil of Egypt. Wesley draws the principle out: God will be behindhand with none who do any service for him, and none shall kindle a fire at his altar for nought; he also catches the strangeness of the last clause, that God’s work was being done by the Babylonians though they thought nothing less. Ellicott notes that the phrase rendered I will give is a participle, literally I am giving, a form used of the immediate future, so the word seems to have been spoken at the very time of the campaign.

Because the conquest itself has been called in question, Ellicott sets out the evidence. It is admitted by all that Pharaoh-Hophra was dethroned, died a violent death, and was succeeded by Amasis. The account the Egyptian priests gave to Herodotus makes no mention of foreign interference and represents the revolution as wholly internal, caused by a revolt of the troops of Hophra, who sent Amasis to bring them back to their allegiance and was answered by their saluting him as king. He calls that authority suspicious, since the priests were prone to cover up whatever told against the honour of their country, and since the popularity of Amasis with the troops and his unpopularity with the people are scarcely consistent. He then turns to the prophets: Jeremiah has a full prophecy of the same conquest, was afterwards carried into Egypt and there uttered others to the same effect, and was probably still living there at the time of the expedition, so that it is inconceivable he should have let them stand on record if the event had proved them false.

The budding horn is referred to almost as many persons as there are commentators. Clarke takes it generally of the restoration and particularly of Zerubbabel, but allows that it may respect Daniel, or Mordecai, or Jeconiah, who about this time was brought out of prison by Evil-merodach. Wesley names Jehoiakim instead, advanced by the same king. Gill canvasses the whole range: not the time of Egypt’s destruction, unless it means the advancement of Daniel at Babylon or the taking of Jehoiachin out of prison, but rather the restoration forty years after, when Cyrus proclaimed liberty to the Jews to return and build their city and temple under Zerubbabel their prince; and he adds that it need not be limited to either, but may regard the day when the kingdom of Israel should flourish spiritually under the Messiah, the Horn of salvation and Branch of David. Ellicott alone declines to name a man. The tenses change to the future, showing that the consequences to Israel were to develop only gradually: first the conviction that trust in any earthly aid is futile, then a turning to their neglected God, and as a result the giving up of their long cherished idolatries, spoken of as only in germ under the figure of a horn budding forth. As for the opening of the mouth, promised elsewhere as a consequence of the fall of Jerusalem, he observes that no prophecy of this prophet is recorded of later date, so the expression must mean the encouraging instructions he gave as the people improved under the discipline of the captivity, which it was not seen fitting to put on permanent record.
